### Evaluating generated text against references A translation can express the right meaning without using the reference's words. Conversely, a candidate can reuse most of the reference while changing a name, a number or a negation. Reference-based metrics specify which kinds of similarity receive credit; they do not directly observe whether the source meaning has been preserved. Consider the candidate “the cat is on the mat” and the reference “the cat is on a mat”. They share words and several consecutive phrases. The calculation below follows those matches from individual counts to a corpus-level BLEU score. Word boundaries are supplied explicitly, so tokenization is separate from the counting algorithm. #### BLEU: clipped counts and local word order For an $n$-gram $g$, let $C_i(g)$ count its occurrences in candidate segment $i$, and let $R_{ij}(g)$ count its occurrences in reference $j$ for that segment. A segment can have several human references. Its maximum reference count is $$ M_i(g)=\max_j R_{ij}(g). $$ The credited count is $\min(C_i(g), M_i(g))$. Repeating a matching word does not create unlimited credit. In the original paper's repeated-“the” example, the candidate has seven copies; no single reference contains more than two. Modified unigram precision is therefore 2/7. Counts from different references are not added together. [Papineni et al., §2.1](https://aclanthology.org/P02-1040.pdf#page=2). The same rule applies to whole sequences of two, three or four tokens. For the six-token cat example, the sufficient statistics are: | Order | Credited candidate n-grams | Total candidate n-grams | Precision | |---|---|---:|---:| | 1 | the, cat, is, on, mat; only one of the two copies of “the” receives credit | 6 | 5/6 | | 2 | the cat; cat is; is on | 5 | 3/5 | | 3 | the cat is; cat is on | 4 | 2/4 | | 4 | the cat is on | 3 | 1/3 | Matches can occur at different positions in the two strings, but the words inside an n-gram must be consecutive and in the same order. Unigrams alone cannot distinguish a bag of the right words from a fluent phrase. Longer matches preserve local order, while still missing dependencies outside their window. For a test corpus, clip counts separately within each aligned segment, then add the clipped numerators and the candidate denominators: $$ p_n= \frac{\sum_i\sum_{g\in G_n(h_i)}\min(C_i(g),M_i(g))} {\sum_i\sum_{g\in G_n(h_i)}C_i(g)}. $$ Here $G_n(h_i)$ contains distinct $n$-grams; $C_i(g)$ supplies their multiplicities. A reference for a different source segment cannot license a match. If two candidates are “a” and “b”, while their respective references are “b” and “a”, neither candidate matches. Pooling all words across the corpus would incorrectly award both matches. #### Brevity penalty and the complete score A two-word fragment copied from a long reference can have perfect unigram and bigram precision while omitting most of the translation. BLEU multiplies the precision score by a brevity penalty. For each candidate, select the reference length closest to its own length; the sacreBLEU implementation uses the shorter reference on an equal-distance tie. Sum those selected lengths to obtain $r$, and sum candidate lengths to obtain $c$: $$ BP= \begin{cases} 1,&c\ge r,\\ \exp(1-r/c),&0 #### chrF: matching characters instead of whole words A word-level metric treats “cat” and “cats” as different tokens. A character metric can still match their shared letters and adjacent character pairs. For the candidate “cat” and reference “cats”, unigram character precision is 3/3 and recall is 3/4; bigram precision is 2/2 and recall is 2/3. A two-order example averages these to $P=1$ and $R=17/24$. The F-beta combination is $$ F_\beta=\frac{(1+\beta^2)PR}{\beta^2P+R}. $$ With $\beta=2$, the two-order example gives $85/113\approx0.7522$. This puts more weight on recall than $F_1$ does. It does not prove that dropping the final “s” preserves meaning: the metric has retained a partial surface match. In sacreBLEU 2.5.1, standard chrF uses up to six character orders, $\beta=2$ and no word $n$-grams. The example above explicitly uses only two character orders. The default implementation averages precision and recall over orders with nonempty candidate and reference counts, then combines them. Its epsilon-smoothing option uses another aggregation convention. For multiple references it selects one segment's reference statistics by the best F-score, rather than constructing BLEU's per-n-gram maximum counts. ChrF++ additionally includes word unigrams and bigrams when `word_order=2`. [Popović, chrF](https://aclanthology.org/W15-3049/); [versioned chrF implementation](https://github.com/mjpost/sacrebleu/blob/d4d9a26dd833fe23696e09ca2a70b2fc433f3d4b/sacrebleu/metrics/chrf.py). #### BERTScore: contextual token matching Replacing “cold” with “freezing” eliminates an exact word match, even though the two expressions may describe related conditions. BERTScore encodes each complete sentence with a pretrained contextual encoder. After normalizing the token vectors, it builds their pairwise cosine similarity matrix. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/bleu-reconciliation-2026-10-30/bert-score-recall.png]] *Tianyi Zhang, Varsha Kishore, Felix Wu, Kilian Q. Weinberger and Yoav Artzi, [BERTScore original overview](https://github.com/Tiiiger/bert_score/blob/19e7f551fe4fa43fdd07b8129ae947015b902b2d/README.md#overview). Complete original image, copied without cropping, redrawing or translation. Copyright © 2019 the authors, [MIT License](/licenses/bertscore-19e7f551-MIT.txt).* Each reference token takes the largest value in its row to obtain recall; each candidate token takes the largest value in its column to obtain precision. The unweighted scores average those maxima. In this orientation, $$ \begin{gathered} R_{\rm BERT}=\frac1k\sum_i\max_j s_{ij},\\ P_{\rm BERT}=\frac1l\sum_j\max_i s_{ij},\\ F_{\rm BERT}=\frac{2PR}{P+R}. \end{gathered} $$ These matches are many-to-one: “weather” and “cold” both select “freezing” in the original figure. The algorithm does not consume the chosen token or solve a one-to-one assignment problem. The token representations depend on the rest of each sentence, but the maximum operation itself provides no proof of equivalence, factual correctness or preserved negation. The figure weights reference tokens by inverse document frequency. Common tokens receive less weight; the displayed IDF of “the” is 1.27, while “weather” has 7.94. Weighted recall divides the weighted sum of row maxima by the sum of reference weights: $$ R_{\rm BERT,IDF} =\frac{\sum_i w_i\max_j s_{ij}}{\sum_i w_i}. $$ Using the rounded values printed in the image: ```python import math # Rounded cosine similarities and reference IDF weights printed in the source figure. similarity = [ [0.713, 0.597, 0.428, 0.408], [0.462, 0.393, 0.515, 0.326], [0.635, 0.858, 0.441, 0.441], [0.479, 0.454, 0.796, 0.343], [0.347, 0.361, 0.307, 0.913], ] reference_idf = [1.27, 7.94, 1.82, 7.90, 8.88] best_reference_matches = [max(row) for row in similarity] weighted_recall = sum(w * score for w, score in zip(reference_idf, best_reference_matches)) / sum(reference_idf) precision = sum(max(column) for column in zip(*similarity)) / len(similarity[0]) recall = sum(best_reference_matches) / len(similarity) f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) assert round(weighted_recall, 3) == 0.753 assert math.isclose(precision, 0.82) assert math.isclose(recall, 0.759) print('weighted recall:', weighted_recall) print('unweighted P, R, F1:', precision, recall, f1) ``` The weighted result rounds to the figure's 0.753. The printed unweighted $P$, $R$ and $F_1$ form a separate, consistently unweighted calculation; combining weighted recall with unweighted precision would be another metric. No encoder or pretrained model runs in this arithmetic example. The encoder checkpoint, layer, tokenizer, IDF corpus and special-token handling affect the scores. Baseline rescaling is another explicit option: for a fixed baseline $b$, a score $S$ becomes $(S-b)/(1-b)$. This is not a new matching procedure or a conversion into percentage accuracy, and rescaled values need not all be positive. Implementations rescale the computed $P$, $R$ and $F$ components separately; rescaled $F$ is not obtained by taking the harmonic mean of rescaled $P$ and $R$. [Zhang et al., §3](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.09675v3#S3). METEOR uses linguistic matching resources such as stems and synonyms; BLEURT and COMET learn scoring functions from supervised data. Their training data, language coverage and evaluation checkpoints become part of the measurement protocol. They should be selected and validated against the required human judgments, rather than treated as interchangeable semantic correctness checkers. [METEOR](https://aclanthology.org/W05-0909/), [BLEURT](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.704/), [COMET](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.213/). For answers with verifiable facts or executable outcomes, reference similarity is only one observation. The next section explains how a judge adds a rubric and its own failure modes; the earlier functional-checking example measures program behavior rather than overlap with one reference. ### Судья на основе языковой модели
